questions.q: Where does a value like `${{ secrets.DB_PASSWORD }}` actually come from?
options: A secret configured on GitHub itself, in repository Settings — never written in the repository's files
A plain text file committed to the repository
The workflow file's own comments
An environment variable set on the developer's personal laptop only
questions.explain: Secrets are configured through GitHub's Settings UI and injected at run time — they never appear in any committed file.

questions.q: What happens when you try to view a previously saved GitHub secret's value?
options: You can't — GitHub can only let you overwrite it, never display the saved value again
GitHub shows it in plain text after a confirmation prompt
It's emailed to the repository owner automatically
It's displayed in the workflow's run log by default
questions.explain: Secrets are encrypted at rest — there's no 'reveal' feature, only the ability to overwrite an existing secret with a new value.

questions.q: What does GitHub do automatically if a workflow step accidentally prints a secret's value in its output?
options: Masks it as *** in the log
Immediately deletes the entire repository
Sends an alert to every collaborator
Nothing — secrets are printed in plain text like any other value
questions.explain: GitHub automatically masks any secret value that appears in workflow logs, replacing it with asterisks.

questions.q: Are secrets passed to a workflow triggered by a pull request from a fork, by default?
options: No — they are withheld by default, protecting against a malicious PR trying to exfiltrate credentials
Yes, always, with no restrictions
Only if the fork's owner requests access
Only secrets named PROD_* are withheld; all others are always passed
questions.explain: GitHub withholds secrets from fork-triggered pull request workflows by default, exactly to prevent credential exfiltration via a malicious PR.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend separate secrets for CI (like DB_PASSWORD) and production (like PROD_DB_PASSWORD)?
options: So a bug or compromised dependency in a PR's CI run can't reach production data, since the CI credential can't access it
Because GitHub technically only allows one secret per repository
There's no real reason — it's just a naming convention with no security benefit
To make the workflow file longer for readability
questions.explain: Scoping the CI credential to only a disposable schema, separate from the production credential, limits the blast radius if something in CI misbehaves.
